source_refs.note: PDF 220 (book p. 218): 7.1.1 Scalars, definition and the examples distance and speed

blocks.text: Scalar quantities are those that are completely described by magnitude only (size or numerical value). Scalars do not have direction.

items: Distance: Total length of the path travelled, regardless of direction.
Speed: Rate at which distance is covered per unit time, irrespective of direction.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"Magnitude" means a number together with its unit, for example 5 km or 20 m/s. For a scalar, that is the whole story: 5 km of walking is 5 km whichever way you walked.
Distance adds up every piece of the path, so it can only grow or stay the same as time passes, and it is never negative.
Speed is distance per unit time: \(\text{speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}\). Its common units are m/s and km/h. Since
\[1\ \text{km/h} = \dfrac{1000\ \text{m}}{3600\ \text{s}}\]
\[= \dfrac{5}{18}\ \text{m/s},\]
multiply by \(\frac{5}{18}\) to change km/h into m/s (for example \(36\) km/h \(= 10\) m/s), and by \(\frac{18}{5}\) to go back. You will need this in the exercise.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A scalar has magnitude only (number + unit) and no direction.
2. Distance = total length of the path travelled; it is never negative.
3. Speed = distance covered per unit time; it is never negative.
4. \(1\) km/h \(= \frac{5}{18}\) m/s.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing a negative distance or a negative speed. Neither can be negative; a minus sign belongs only to vector quantities such as displacement and velocity (7.1.2).
2. Mixing units, for example dividing kilometres by seconds, or minutes by hours, without converting first.
